docs.title: metafopy gives a value where R does not
emmprep() of an rma_mh fit
docs.text:
R's emmprep gives an estimate of 0 with standard error 0 for rma_mh (and rma_peto) fits, and fails for selmodel fits. metafopy computes the estimated marginal mean from the fit.

Why: R's result is a placeholder, not an estimate (the pooled log risk ratio of these data is -0.47). A port that reproduced zeros would give a misleading answer.

R, metafor 5.2-1

library(metafor)
library(emmeans)
res <- rma.mh(ai = tpos, bi = tneg, ci = cpos, di = cneg, data = dat.bcg)
emmeans(emmprep(res), ~ 1)

 1       emmean SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
 overall      0  0 Inf         0         0

Results are given on the log (not the response) scale. 
Confidence level used: 0.95

Python, metafopy

from metafopy import datasets, emmeans, emmprep, rma_mh

res = rma_mh(ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
print(emmeans(emmprep(res), '~ 1'))

 1       emmean    SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
 overall -0.473 0.041 Inf    -0.554    -0.393

Results are given on the log (not the response) scale. 
Confidence level used: 0.95

docs.title: fmtx(drop0ifint=TRUE)
docs.text:
R drops trailing zeros only when digits is an integer (2L); a double 2 does not. Python has no 2 against 2L, so metafopy always drops them.

R, metafor 5.2-1

library(metafor)
fmtx(c(1, 2.5, 3.25), digits = 2, drop0ifint = TRUE)
fmtx(c(1, 2.5, 3.25), digits = 2L, drop0ifint = TRUE)

[1] 1.00 2.50 3.25
[1]    1  2.5 3.25

Python, metafopy

from metafopy import fmtx

print(fmtx([1, 2.5, 3.25], digits=2, drop0ifint=True))

[1]    1  2.5 3.25

docs.title: blup() of a cluster-robust fit recycles quantiles
docs.text:
For a robust(..., club_sandwich=True) fit, R computes the prediction interval of study i with the quantile of coefficient i (modulo the number of coefficients), and warns that the lengths do not match. This is probably a bug in R. metafopy follows it on purpose, gives the same warning, and the two print the same intervals (study 1: -2.4384 to 0.4335; the normal quantile would give -1.5480 to -0.4570).

R, metafor 5.2-1

library(metafor)
dat <- escalc(measure="RR", ai=tpos, bi=tneg, ci=cpos, di=cneg, data=dat.bcg)
res <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data=dat)
rr <- robust(res, cluster=alloc, clubSandwich=TRUE)
head(blup(rr), 2)

     pred     se   pi.lb  pi.ub 
1 -1.0025 0.2783 -2.4384 0.4335 
2 -1.4157 0.2747 -3.0415 0.2101 

Warning messages:
1: In crit * se :
  longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length
2: In crit * se :
  longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length

Python, metafopy

from metafopy import blup, datasets, escalc, rma, robust

dat = escalc(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ ablat', data=dat)
rr = robust(res, cluster=dat['alloc'], club_sandwich=True)
print(blup(rr)[:2])

UserWarning: longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length

1 -1.0025 0.2783 -2.4384 0.4335
2 -1.4157 0.2747 -3.0415 0.2101

res <- rma(yi, vi, data=dat)

rstandard(rr)

docs.title: Coming from R
docs.text: metafopy is built so that metafor code translates line by line. This page lists the rules of the translation. Where metafopy does not behave like metafor, see Differences from metafor, which is kept up to date with every known deviation.

docs.title: The same analysis in both languages
docs.text:
R:

library(metafor)
dat <- escalc(measure="RR", ai=tpos, bi=tneg, ci=cpos, di=cneg, data=dat.bcg)
res <- rma(yi, vi, mods = ~ ablat, data=dat)
print(res)
predict(res, newmods=c(10, 30, 50), transf=exp)
confint(res)
forest(res, atransf=exp)

res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ ablat', data=dat)
print(res)
print(predict(res, newmods=[10, 30, 50], transf=numpy.exp))
print(confint(res))
forest(res, atransf=numpy.exp)

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
In R In metafopy rma.uni, rma.mv, leave1out rma_uni, rma_mv, leave1out: . becomes _ ci.lb, tau2, QE ci_lb, tau2, QE: fields of the result, . becomes _ res$beta, res$se, coef(res) res.beta, res.se dat.bcg (lazy-loaded) datasets.load('dat.bcg') tpos, tneg (unquoted columns, data=dat) 'tpos', 'tneg' (strings naming columns of data=) or arrays mods = ~ ablat + year mods='~ ablat + year' (a string; formulaic syntax) random = ~ 1 \| study/esid random='~ 1 \| study/esid' random = list(~ 1 \| a, ~ 1 \| b) random=['~ 1 \| a', '~ 1 \| b'] btt = 2:3 (1-based) btt=[1, 2] (0-based) subset = year > 1950 subset=dat['year'] > 1950 (a boolean array) transf = exp transf=numpy.exp TRUE / FALSE, NULL, NA True / False, None, numpy.nan control = list(tau2.max = 10) control={'tau2_max': 10}, or a Control / MVControl instance set.seed(1234) set_seed(1234) (R's generator, so permutation tests reproduce R) summary(res) res.summary(): print(res) plus the fit-statistics table (str(res) is print(res)) plot(res) family, forest(res) functions on matplotlib axes: forest, funnel, plot_infl...

Names that metafor writes with . in the middle of a word also lose it in prefixed functions: plot.gosh is plot_gosh, plot.infl.rma.uni is plot_infl, plot.profile.rma is plot_profile, plot.selmodel is plot_selmodel, and transf.ilogit is transf_ilogit. The transformations are also a module: transf.ilogit is metafopy.transf.ilogit (the same function as metafopy.transf_ilogit), so from metafopy import transf keeps metafor's spelling.

docs.title: Classes and generic functions
docs.text: R's S3 classes (rma.uni, rma.mv, escalc...) become frozen dataclasses (RMAResult, RMAMVResult...) and escalc returns a plain pandas.DataFrame whose attrs carry the attributes metafor stores on the data frame. R's generic functions (predict, confint, anova, profile, influence...) are single-dispatch functions that choose the implementation from the class of the result. predict(res, ...) works as in R. The implementations for each class are documented in the reference.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text: metafopy is validated against metafor 5.2-1. The test suite compares the results of the models with R fixtures: closed-form quantities agree to rounding error, and quantities found by numerical optimisation agree to the optimiser's tolerance. The exact tolerances and the cases that differ more are in Differences from metafor.

docs.title: What is not ported
docs.text: reporter() is not ported. emmprep and emmeans' reference grid, marginal means and contrasts are ported natively; see the guide. See Differences from metafor for details and for the places where a metafor feature behaves differently.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
This page takes one dataset from raw 2x2 tables to a pooled estimate, a meta-regression and two plots. Every code block on the page runs as shown.

The data are the BCG vaccine trials of Colditz et al. (1994), https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1994.03510330076038: for each trial the number of tuberculosis cases and non-cases among vaccinated (tpos, tneg) and control (cpos, cneg) subjects, with the absolute latitude of the trial site (ablat).

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Function and argument names are metafor's, with . replaced by _. rma.uni is rma_uni, and rma is an alias.
  • Columns of data are given by name ('yi', 'vi') or as arrays. Moderators are a formula string (mods='~ ablat') or a matrix.
  • Indices are 0-based in code (btt=[1]), while printed output counts from 1, as metafor does.
  • A fitted model is a frozen dataclass. print(res) gives metafor's summary, and the fields hold the numbers (res.beta, res.se, res.tau2, res.I2).
  • The functions you call on a fit are the same as in R: predict, confint, anova, profile, influence and so on.

docs.title: Effect sizes
docs.text:
escalc turns the raw counts into log risk ratios (yi) and their sampling variances (vi):

from metafopy import datasets, escalc

bcg = datasets.load('dat.bcg')
dat = escalc(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=bcg)
print(dat[['trial', 'author', 'year', 'yi', 'vi']].head())

1      2      Ferguson & Simes  1949 -1.585389  0.194581
2      3       Rosenthal et al  1960 -1.348073  0.415368
3      4     Hart & Sutherland  1977 -1.441551  0.020010
4      5  Frimodt-Moller et al  1973 -0.217547  0.051210

docs.title: A random-effects model
docs.text:
from metafopy import rma

res = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat)
print(res)

Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.3132 (SE = 0.1664)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5597
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   92.22%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  12.86

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 12) = 152.2330, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The default heterogeneity estimator is REML, as in metafor. Choose another with method, for example rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat, method='DL'). Pick the tests and intervals with test='knha' (Knapp-Hartung) or level=90.

The numbers are fields of the result:

print(res.beta, res.se, res.tau2, res.I2)

[-0.71453235] [0.17978153] 0.3132433259808949 92.22138607496555

docs.title: Back-transform and predict
docs.text:
The pooled log risk ratio is hard to read. predict takes a transformation:

import numpy

from metafopy import predict

print(predict(res, transf=numpy.exp))

     pred   ci.lb   ci.ub   pi.lb  pi.ub
0  0.4894  0.3441  0.6962  0.1546  1.549

The columns pi.lb and pi.ub are the prediction interval: where the true effect of a new trial would fall.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.14.7 or later, below 3.15.
  • No R installation. The reference numbers from R are committed as fixtures and are only needed by the test suite.

metafopy depends on NumPy, SciPy, pandas, formulaic (model formulas such as '~ ablat') and matplotlib (plots). They are installed with it.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
metafopy is pre-release and is not on PyPI yet. Install it from GitHub with pip or uv:

pip install "metafopy @ git+https://github.com/bnomis/metafopy"
# or
uv add "metafopy @ git+https://github.com/bnomis/metafopy"

To work on metafopy itself, clone the repository and follow the development section of the README.

docs.title: Interactive charts (optional)
docs.text:
The showcase notebook draws linked, interactive charts with Altair. Install the interactive extra to run it (it adds Altair and vl-convert, which saves the charts as SVG or PNG):

pip install "metafopy[interactive] @ git+https://github.com/bnomis/metafopy"

Results also render as HTML tables in Jupyter, which needs no extra.

docs.title: Selection models
docs.text:
Selection models (Vevea and Hedges, 1995, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02294384) model how the probability that a study is published depends on its p-value, and estimate the effect corrected for that selection. selmodel takes a fitted rma_uni model and a selection function type. It mirrors metafor's selmodel; see Citkowicz and Vevea (2017), https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000119, for the parametric functions.

from metafopy import datasets, rma, selmodel

dat = datasets.load('dat.hackshaw1998')
res = rma(data=dat, method='ML')
print(selmodel(res, type='halfnorm'))

Random-Effects Model (k = 37; tau^2 estimator: ML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0321 (SE = 0.0262)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.1792

Test for Heterogeneity:
LRT(df = 1) = 5.0652, p-val = 0.0244

Model Results:

estimate      se    zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub
  0.1011  0.1175  0.8608  0.3894  -0.1291  0.3313

Test for Selection Model Parameters:
LRT(df = 1) = 2.5337, p-val = 0.1114

Selection Model Results:

estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub
  2.0287  1.4126  1.4361  0.1510  0.0000  4.7974

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The first part of the output is the corrected random-effects model. The test of the selection model parameters asks whether there is evidence for selection at all.

The type can be a parametric function ('beta', 'halfnorm', 'negexp', 'logistic', 'power', 'negexppow') or a step function. Step functions need the cut points of the p-value, given as steps:

print(selmodel(res, type='stepfun', steps=[0.025, 0.10, 0.50, 1]))

0.5   < p <= 1       6    0.0618  0.0689  -13.6171  <.0001  0.0000  0.1969  ***

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Each row of the table is the relative probability of publication of a study with a p-value in that interval, relative to the first interval. alternative sets the direction of the one-sided test that selection is based on (default 'greater').

Results can be plotted with plot_selmodel, which draws the estimated selection function. confint, profile, anova and predict work on a selection model fit, and the profile function takes the parallel options of metafor.

Selection models are sensitive to the choice of function and need many studies to be estimated reliably. Use them as a sensitivity analysis. See also Publication bias.

docs.title: Location-scale models
docs.text:
Location-scale models (Viechtbauer and Lopez-Lopez, 2022, https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1562) let the amount of heterogeneity depend on moderators, so tau^2 is modelled alongside the average effect. Pass a scale formula to rma:

from metafopy import rma

dat = datasets.load('dat.bangertdrowns2004')
res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ length', scale='~ length', data=dat)
print(res)

Location-Scale Model (k = 46; tau^2 estimator: REML)

Test for Residual Heterogeneity:
QE(df = 44) = 96.2810, p-val < .0001

Test of Location Coefficients (coefficient 2):
QM(df = 1) = 4.2107, p-val = 0.0402

Model Results (Location):

         estimate      se    zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub
intrcpt    0.0719  0.0766  0.9392  0.3476  -0.0782  0.2220
length     0.0149  0.0073  2.0520  0.0402   0.0007  0.0292  *

Test of Scale Coefficients (coefficient 2):
QM(df = 1) = 0.4194, p-val = 0.5172

Model Results (Scale):

         estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub
intrcpt   -3.6011  0.9112  -3.9520  <.0001  -5.3870  -1.8151  ***
length     0.0472  0.0728   0.6476  0.5172  -0.0956   0.1899

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The location part (the average effect) and the scale part (the log of tau^2, by default) are reported separately. Use link='identity' to model tau^2 itself. The result is an RMALSResult, and predict, confint, anova (Wald and likelihood ratio tests), profile, vif, blup, ranef, rstandard and permutest work on it.

control={'optimizer': ...} accepts the optimisers of rma.uni ('optim' with optmethod, 'nlm', 'bobyqa', 'hjk', ..., and with link='identity' also 'constrOptim', 'solnp', 'nloptr', 'constrOptim.nl'/'alabama' and 'auglag'; any other optimiser is reset to 'constrOptim' with a warning there, and the barrier optimisers cannot be used with the log link). They are mapped as for selmodel; ncpus above 1 selects 'optimParallel', but the likelihood is evaluated serially. confint(res, control={'vc.min': ..., 'vc.max': ...}) sets the interval searched for the bounds (vc_min and vc_max work too).

from metafopy import predict

print(predict(res, newmods=[5, 25], newscale=[5, 25]))

     pred      se   ci.lb   ci.ub   pi.lb   pi.ub
1  0.1466  0.0516  0.0455  0.2477 -0.2315  0.5247
2  0.4454  0.1278  0.1949  0.6960 -0.1899  1.0807

docs.title: Publication bias
docs.text:
Small-study effects and publication bias distort the pooled estimate when studies with small or non-significant effects are less likely to be published. No method can prove that there is no bias; use several as sensitivity analyses, together with a funnel plot. Sterne et al. (2011), https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.d4002, give recommendations.

The examples use the passive smoking data of Hackshaw et al.:

from metafopy import datasets, rma

dat = datasets.load('dat.hackshaw1998')
res = rma(data=dat)

The data already hold yi and vi, so rma(data=dat) needs no column names.

docs.title: Regression test
docs.text:
The regression test of Egger et al. (1997), https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.315.7109.629, regresses the effects on their standard errors. A slope that differs from zero indicates funnel plot asymmetry. The default model is metafor's model='rma' (a weighted regression with a random-effects component). predictor chooses the predictor: 'sei', 'vi', 'ni' or 'ninv', and model='lm' gives the classical test.

from metafopy import regtest

print(regtest(res))
print(regtest(res, model='lm'))

Regression Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry

Model:     mixed-effects meta-regression model
Predictor: standard error

Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry: z = 2.1055, p = 0.0352
Limit Estimate (as sei -> 0):   b = 0.0216 (CI: -0.1774, 0.2207)


Regression Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry

Model:     weighted regression with multiplicative dispersion
Predictor: standard error

Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry: t = 2.3824, df = 35, p = 0.0228
Limit Estimate (as sei -> 0):   b = 0.0050 (CI: -0.1694, 0.1794)

docs.title: Rank correlation test
docs.text:
Begg and Mazumdar's (1994), https://doi.org/10.2307/2533446, test is the rank correlation between standardized effects and their variances:

from metafopy import ranktest

print(ranktest(res))

Rank Correlation Test for Funnel Plot Asymmetry

Kendall's tau = 0.1441, p = 0.2157

docs.title: Trim and fill
docs.text:
Trim and fill (Duval and Tweedie, 2000, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.0006-341X.2000.00455.x) estimates the number of missing studies on one side of the funnel plot, adds them, and re-estimates the pooled effect. It applies to models without moderators.

from metafopy import trimfill

tf = trimfill(res)
print(tf)

Estimated number of missing studies on the left side: 7 (SE = 4.0399)

Random-Effects Model (k = 44; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0245 (SE = 0.0182)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.1564
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   28.80%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  1.40

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 43) = 60.4755, p-val = 0.0404

Model Results:

estimate      se    zval    pval   ci.lb   ci.ub
  0.1745  0.0484  3.6024  0.0003  0.0795  0.2694  ***

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Choose side='left' or 'right' to fix the side with the missing studies and estimator ('L0', 'R0', 'Q0'). The filled data show in a funnel plot with funnel(tf).

docs.title: Fail-safe N
docs.text:
The fail-safe N is the number of unpublished null studies that would be needed to make the pooled result non-significant. fsn offers the type values 'Rosenthal', 'Orwin', 'Rosenberg', 'General' (the default for model fits) and 'Binomial'. The method has been criticised, see Becker (2005), https://doi.org/10.1002/0470870168.ch7, and trimfill and selection models are usually preferable.

from metafopy import fsn

print(fsn(res))

Fail-safe N Calculation Using the General Approach

Average Effect Size:         0.2189 (with file drawer: 0.0473)
Amount of Heterogeneity:     0.0224 (with file drawer: 0.0312)
Observed Significance Level: <.0001 (with file drawer: 0.0504)
Target Significance Level:   0.05

Fail-safe N: 112

docs.title: Test of excess significance
docs.text:
tes tests whether more studies are significant than their power would suggest (Ioannidis and Trikalinos, 2007, https://doi.org/10.1177/1740774507079441):

from metafopy import tes

print(tes(res))

Test of Excess Significance

Observed Number of Significant Findings: 7 (out of 37)
Expected Number of Significant Findings: 7.0244
Observed Number / Expected Number:       0.9965

Estimated Power of Tests (based on theta = 0.2189)

   min      q1  median      q3     max
0.0652  0.0933  0.1476  0.2685  0.5605

Test of Excess Significance: p = 0.5041 (X^2 = 0.0001, df = 1)
Limit Estimate (theta_lim):  0.1028 (where p = 0.1)

docs.title: Henmi-Copas interval
docs.text:
hc gives a confidence interval for a random-effects model that is robust to small-study effects and has better coverage than the Wald interval when the number of studies is small (Henmi and Copas, 2010, https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.4029):

from metafopy import hc

print(hc(res))

    method   tau2 estimate     se  ci.lb  ci.ub
rma   REML 0.0224   0.2189 0.0494 0.1221 0.3157
hc      DL 0.0170   0.1858 0.0493 0.0830 0.2885

docs.title: Selection models
docs.text: For a model-based correction use selmodel.

docs.title: Binary and count data
docs.text:
For 2x2 tables (events and non-events in a treatment and a control group) and for event counts with person-time, the data can be analysed in several ways. All of them take the raw counts, so you do not call escalc yourself.

Function Method Measures rma_uni Inverse-variance, on escalc effect sizes any rma_mh Mantel-Haenszel OR, RR, RD, IRR, IRD rma_peto Peto's one-step method OR rma_glmm Generalized linear mixed-effects models OR, IRR, PLO, IRLN and the experimental measures

The arguments are the same throughout: ai, bi, ci, di for the cells of the table (events and non-events in the treatment and control group), or ai, n1i, ci, n2i with the group sizes, and data=.

docs.title: Mantel-Haenszel
docs.text:
Mantel-Haenszel pooling (Mantel and Haenszel, 1959, https://doi.org/10.1093/jnci/22.4.719) behaves well with sparse data, and needs no continuity correction for studies with a zero in a single cell. It is an equal-effects method.

from metafopy import datasets, rma_mh

bcg = datasets.load('dat.bcg')
print(rma_mh(ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=bcg, measure='RR'))

Equal-Effects Model (k = 13)

I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):  92.13%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability): 12.71

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 12) = 152.5676, p-val < .0001

Model Results (log scale):

estimate      se      zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub
 -0.4537  0.0393  -11.5338  <.0001  -0.5308  -0.3766

Model Results (RR scale):

estimate   ci.lb   ci.ub
  0.6353  0.5881  0.6862

docs.title: Peto's method
docs.text:
Peto's method (Yusuf et al., 1985, https://doi.org/10.1016/S0033-0620(85)80003-7) works on the observed minus expected number of events and is accurate for rare events and balanced groups:

from metafopy import rma_peto

print(rma_peto(ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=bcg))

Equal-Effects Model (k = 13)

I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):  92.85%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability): 13.98

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 12) = 167.7302, p-val < .0001

Model Results (log scale):

estimate      se      zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub
 -0.4744  0.0407  -11.6689  <.0001  -0.5541  -0.3948

Model Results (OR scale):

estimate   ci.lb   ci.ub
  0.6222  0.5746  0.6738

docs.title: Generalized linear mixed-effects models
docs.text:
rma_glmm fits the exact binomial or Poisson likelihood with random effects, which avoids the normal approximation and the continuity corrections of the inverse-variance method. This is the best choice for sparse data, and it is slower. Choose the model with model: 'UM.FS' and 'UM.RS' are unconditional models with fixed or random study effects, 'CM.AL' and 'CM.EL' are conditional models (approximate and exact likelihood). See Stijnen et al. (2010), https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.4040.

from metafopy import rma_glmm

print(rma_glmm(ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=bcg, measure='OR', model='UM.FS'))

Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: ML)
Model Type: Unconditional Model with Fixed Study Effects

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.2949
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5430
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   91.02%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  11.14

Tests for Heterogeneity:
Wld(df = 12) = 163.1649, p-val < .0001
LRT(df = 12) = 176.9544, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub
 -0.7450  0.1756  -4.2436  <.0001  -1.0891  -0.4009  ***

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

rma_glmm accepts moderators (mods='~ ablat'). predict, blup and ranef work on its result. Mixed-model fits can differ slightly from R, because lme4 stops at a looser optimiser tolerance; see Differences from metafor.

As in metafor, control={'package': 'GLMMadaptive'} fits the mixed models with adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature (Pinheiro and Bates, 1995; GLMMadaptive) and control={'package': 'glmmTMB'} with the Laplace approximation (Brooks et al., 2017); nAGQ is ignored by glmmTMB.

For the conditional model CM.EL with method='FE', control={'optimizer': 'clogit'} or 'clogistic' fit it with the partial likelihood of survival::clogit or Epi::clogistic. link= and family= change the link function or the family of the unconditional models.

The other optimisers of rma.glmm are available for CM.EL too (control={'optimizer': 'BFGS'}, 'Nelder-Mead', or 'optim' with optmethod=, optCtrl={'maxit': ...}, and 'CG', 'L-BFGS-B', 'nlm', 'bobyqa', ...). optim's BFGS and Nelder-Mead are exact ports of R's routines; the rest use the closest SciPy method. control={'hesspack': 'pracma'} or 'calculus' (default 'numDeriv') and control={'hessianCtrl': {...}} choose how the Hessian of CM.EL is computed. control={'dnchgcalc': 'dnoncenhypergeom'} or 'dFNCHypergeo' and control={'dnchgprec': 1e-10} choose the density of the non-central hypergeometric distribution; naming 'dFNCHypergeo' or a precision uses a port of BiasedUrn's algorithm, including the truncation of its tails. See differences from metafor for what can differ.

docs.title: Rates
docs.text:
For incidence rates, pass the event counts x1i, x2i and the person-time t1i, t2i, with measure='IRR':

from metafopy import escalc

print(escalc(measure='IRR', x1i=[3, 5], t1i=[100, 120], x2i=[7, 4], t2i=[110, 90])[['yi', 'vi']])

         yi       vi
0 -0.751988  0.47619
1 -0.064539  0.45000

docs.title: Zero cells
docs.text: Studies with a zero cell need a continuity correction for the inverse-variance method. add, to and drop00 control it and have the same meaning in escalc, rma_uni, rma_mh, rma_peto and rma_glmm. Studies with no events in both groups carry no information about the relative effect and are dropped by rma_mh and rma_peto (drop00=True). Sweeting et al. (2004), https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.1761, discuss the alternatives.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
metafopy ships the datasets of the R package metadat that the metafor examples use. Load one by its R name, with or without the dat. prefix, as a pandas.DataFrame:

from metafopy import datasets

print(datasets.list_datasets()[:5])
dat = datasets.load('dat.bcg')
print(dat.head())
print(datasets.load('bcg').equals(dat))

['dat.assink2016', 'dat.bangertdrowns2004', 'dat.bcg', 'dat.berkey1998', 'dat.cohen1981']
   trial                author  year  tpos  ...  cpos   cneg  ablat      alloc
0      1               Aronson  1948     4  ...    11    128     44     random
1      2      Ferguson & Simes  1949     6  ...    29    274     55     random
2      3       Rosenthal et al  1960     3  ...    11    209     42     random
3      4     Hart & Sutherland  1977    62  ...   248  12619     52     random
4      5  Frimodt-Moller et al  1973    33  ...    47   5761     13  alternate

[5 rows x 9 columns]
True

list_datasets() lists every bundled dataset. Each load returns a fresh copy that you can modify.

The metadat documentation describes the variables and cites the original source of each dataset: https://wviechtb.github.io/metadat/. Columns keep their R names, including dots (or.lb), so use brackets (dat['or.lb']) to access them.

docs.title: Trees
docs.text: dat.moura2021 comes with a phylogenetic tree, loaded with datasets.load_tree('dat.moura2021.tree'). The result is a PhyloTree with the tip labels (tip_labels) and the variance-covariance or correlation matrix of the tips (vcv), which is what rma_mv needs for phylogenetic models. See Multilevel and multivariate models.

docs.title: Using your own data
docs.text: Any DataFrame works. Give column names as strings with data=, or pass arrays directly. Missing values are handled as in metafor: na_action='omit' (the default) drops studies with missing values, 'fail' raises an error.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Diagnostics for rma_uni fits follow metafor's functions of the same names. The examples use the BCG data:

from metafopy import datasets, escalc, rma

dat = escalc(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
res = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat)

rstandard gives internally standardized residuals and rstudent externally studentized residuals (the residual of each study from a model fitted without it). Studies with absolute values above about 2 or 3 deserve a look.

residuals takes a type: 'response' (the default, the raw residuals), 'rstandard', 'rstudent', 'pearson' (the raw residuals divided by the square root of the sampling variance plus tau^2) and 'cholesky' (the residuals decorrelated with the Cholesky factor of the marginal variance-covariance matrix). Which types a fit class allows follows metafor. na_action stands in for R's options(na.action=). weights_(type='matrix') returns the weight matrix.

from metafopy import residuals

print(residuals(res, 'pearson'))
print(res.residuals('rstudent', na_action='exclude'))
print(res.weights_('matrix').shape)

from metafopy import influence

The individual diagnostics are also available as cooks_distance and dfbetas; influence(res, measure='cooks.distance'), measure='dfbetas' and measure='rstudent' return the same objects as those functions and rstudent, as in metafor. plot_infl plots them all:

import matplotlib.pyplot

from metafopy import plot_infl

plot_infl(inf)
matplotlib.pyplot.savefig('influence.png')

docs.title: Leave-one-out and cumulative analyses
docs.text:
leave1out refits the model leaving out each study in turn and cumul adds the studies one at a time, in their order in the data (sort the data first to cumulate by year or precision).

from metafopy import cumul, leave1out

print(leave1out(res).estimate[:3])
print(cumul(res).estimate[:3])

[-0.70708379 -0.6540312  -0.68555442]
[-0.88931133 -1.32500344 -1.33023415]

Both return a result whose fields (estimate, se, ci_lb, ci_ub, tau2...) are arrays with one entry per fit, and print as a table. leave1out and cumul also work for rma_mh and rma_peto fits.

docs.title: Heterogeneity sources: Baujat and GOSH
docs.text:
A Baujat plot (Baujat et al., 2002, https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.1221) shows which studies contribute most to the heterogeneity and to the overall result. The GOSH plot (Olkin et al., 2012, https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1053) fits the model to many subsets of the studies and shows the distribution of the results. With many studies it fits a random sample of the subsets, controlled by subsets and seed.

from metafopy import baujat, gosh, plot_gosh, set_seed

baujat(res)
set_seed(1234)
plot_gosh(gosh(res, subsets=200))

docs.title: Heteroscedastic heterogeneity
docs.text:
The random-effects model assumes the same amount of heterogeneity, tau^2, for every study. hettest (new in metafor 5.2-1) tests this assumption, H0: tau^2_1 = ... = tau^2_k, for a model without moderators or for a vector of estimates with their sampling variances (vi=) or standard errors (sei=). The default is a score test; test='lrt' and test='wald' give a likelihood ratio and a Wald-type test, and 'ksn', 'ksx2', 'adn' and 'adx2' check the Pearson residuals with Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Anderson-Darling goodness-of-fit tests. The p-values come from a parametric bootstrap (boot=1000 samples unless you set boot= to another count), which draws from R's random number generator, so seed= gives the results of set.seed() in R. boot=False uses the chi-squared reference distribution of the three model-based tests instead.

from metafopy import hettest

print(hettest(res, seed=1234))
print(hettest(res, test=['lrt', 'ksn'], boot=200, seed=1234))

Test for Heteroscedastic Heterogeneity

Estimation method: Restricted maximum likelihood
Test type:         Score test
Bootstrapping:     Yes (1000/1000 iterations)

X^2(df = 12) = 2.8884, p = 0.9920

The result holds the statistics (statistic), p-values (pval), the estimated study-specific variances (tau2i) and the bootstrapped statistics (statistic_boot). Fitted models of the classes rma_mv, rma_glmm, selmodel and location-scale models are not accepted, as in metafor.

docs.title: Variance inflation factors
docs.text:
For meta-regression, vif reports collinearity among the moderators:

from metafopy import vif

print(vif(rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ ablat + year', data=dat)))

 ablat    year
1.5391  1.5391

vif also takes rma_mv, location-scale and selmodel fits with moderators. The options are those of metafor: btt (and att for the scale part), table=True for the coefficient table, intercept=True to include the intercept, fixed=True to match a string btt literally, and, except for selmodel fits, reestimate=True and sim.

docs.title: Effect sizes
docs.text: Most analyses start from raw study data (2x2 tables, means and standard deviations, correlations, proportions) that escalc converts to an effect size yi and its sampling variance vi. If the studies already report effect sizes and standard errors, skip escalc and pass them to rma directly.

docs.title: escalc
docs.text:
escalc takes a measure and the arguments that measure needs, and returns a pandas DataFrame. With data= the new columns yi and vi are appended to your data.

from metafopy import datasets, escalc

dat = datasets.load('dat.curtis1998')
dat = escalc(measure='ROM', m1i='m1i', sd1i='sd1i', n1i='n1i', m2i='m2i', sd2i='sd2i', n2i='n2i', data=dat)
print(dat[['id', 'genus', 'species', 'yi', 'vi']].head())

   id    genus    species        yi        vi
0  21    ALNUS      RUBRA  0.550192  0.038472
1  22    ALNUS      RUBRA  0.147040  0.017455
2  27     ACER     RUBRUM  0.437769  0.032753
3  32  QUERCUS     PRINUS -0.110832  0.029516
4  35    MALUS  DOMESTICA  0.117135  0.046786

Here ROM is the log ratio of means, comparing woody plant mass under elevated and ambient CO2, the example of Hedges et al. (1999), https://doi.org/10.1890/0012-9658(1999)080[1150:TMAORR]2.0.CO;2. A ratio of means suits outcomes that are positive and measured on a ratio scale.

The measures are metafor's, with the same abbreviations, and fall into groups by the data they need:

Data Arguments Measures, for example 2x2 tables ai, bi, ci, di (or n1i, n2i with ai, ci) RR, OR, RD, PETO, AS, PHI, YUQ, RTET Person-time x1i, x2i, t1i, t2i IRR, IRD, IRSD Two group means m1i, m2i, sd1i, sd2i, n1i, n2i MD, SMD, SMDH, ROM, VR, CVR Correlations ri, ni COR, ZCOR Proportions xi, ni PR, PLO, PAS, PFT Incidence rates xi, ti IR, IRLN, IRS, IRFT Single means mi, sdi, ni MN, MNLN, SMN, SDLN, CVLN Change scores m1i, m2i, sd1i, sd2i, ni, ri MC, SMCC, SMCR, ROMC Partial and semi-partial correlations, R^2 ri, ti, ni, mi, r2i PCOR, SPCOR, R2, ZR2 Precomputed yi, vi or sei GEN

metafopy.effects.measures.MEASURES is the full list, and the escalc reference the required arguments of each. The metafor documentation describes the formulas: https://wviechtb.github.io/metafor/reference/escalc.html.

docs.title: Zero cells and bias correction
docs.text:
Counts of zero make log ratios undefined. add, to and drop00 control the continuity correction exactly as in metafor: by default 0.5 is added to all four cells of a study that has a zero cell (to='only0'). Set add=0 to turn this off, or to='all' to correct every study.

from metafopy import escalc

zero = datasets.load('dat.hine1989')
print(escalc(measure='OR', ai='ai', n1i='n1i', ci='ci', n2i='n2i', data=zero)[['yi', 'vi']])
print(escalc(measure='OR', ai='ai', n1i='n1i', ci='ci', n2i='n2i', data=zero, add=0)[['yi', 'vi']])

         yi        vi
0  0.819899  1.550837
1  0.000000  0.550000
2  0.453784  0.436002
3  0.326001  0.363800
4  0.847298  0.495608
5  1.004583  0.354944
         yi        vi
0  0.819899  1.550837
1  0.000000  0.550000
2  0.453784  0.436002
3  0.326001  0.363800
4  0.847298  0.495608
5  1.004583  0.354944

Measures such as SMD apply the small-sample bias correction of Hedges (1981), https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986006002107, by default (correct=True). For the choice of sampling variance formula see vtype, described in the metafor documentation.

docs.title: Correlations and proportions
docs.text:
The raw correlation has a variance that depends on the correlation itself. Meta-analyses of correlations therefore work on Fisher's z (ZCOR) and back-transform for presentation, following Borenstein et al. (2009), https://doi.org/10.1002/9780470743386:

import numpy

from metafopy import predict, rma

mol = datasets.load('dat.molloy2014')
mol = escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri='ri', ni='ni', data=mol)
res = rma('yi', 'vi', data=mol)
print(predict(res, transf=numpy.tanh))

     pred   ci.lb   ci.ub   pi.lb   pi.ub
0  0.1488  0.0878  0.2087 -0.0371  0.3248

For proportions, the logit (PLO) is a common choice, with transf.ilogit to go back:

from metafopy import transf

pri = datasets.load('dat.pritz1997')
pri = escalc(measure='PLO', xi='xi', ni='ni', data=pri)
print(predict(rma('yi', 'vi', data=pri), transf=transf.ilogit))

     pred   ci.lb   ci.ub   pi.lb   pi.ub
0  0.7575  0.6605  0.8337  0.4661  0.9179

docs.title: Precomputed effect sizes
docs.text:
If a dataset already has effect sizes and sampling variances, pass them straight to rma, or to escalc with measure='GEN' to attach labels. Standard errors work too, with sei=:

from metafopy import rma

rau = datasets.load('dat.raudenbush1985')
print(rma('yi', 'vi', data=rau))

Random-Effects Model (k = 19; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.0188 (SE = 0.0155)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.1372
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   41.86%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  1.72

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 18) = 35.8295, p-val = 0.0074

Model Results:

estimate      se    zval    pval    ci.lb   ci.ub
  0.0837  0.0516  1.6208  0.1051  -0.0175  0.1849

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

docs.title: Study labels, subsets and flipping
docs.text:
slab gives study labels used in plots and printed output, subset selects studies, and flip changes the sign of the effect size of selected studies. All three accept a column name or an array.

stay = escalc(measure='MD', n1i='n1i', n2i='n2i', m1i='m1i', m2i='m2i', sd1i='sd1i', sd2i='sd2i', data=datasets.load('dat.normand1999'), slab='source')
print(stay.attrs['slab'])

['Edinburgh', 'Orpington-Mild', 'Orpington-Moderate', 'Orpington-Severe', 'Montreal-Home', 'Montreal-Transfer', 'Newcastle', 'Umea', 'Uppsala']

from metafopy import summary_escalc

docs.title: Transformations
docs.text: metafopy.transf holds metafor's transformation functions (transf.ilogit, transf.ztor, transf.dtocles and so on, also imported at the top level as transf_ilogit, transf_ztor, ...). Pass them as transf= to predict and confint, or as atransf= to the plot functions. NumPy functions such as numpy.exp and numpy.tanh work as well.

docs.title: Estimated marginal means
docs.text:
metafopy has a native port of the parts of R's emmeans (Lenth, 2024, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=emmeans) that metafor users reach through emmprep: a reference grid, marginal means (least-squares means) with their covariance matrix, contrasts with multiplicity adjustments, and back-transformation to the scale of the effect size. The results are checked against emmeans together with metafor 5.2-1 on R-generated fixtures.

A marginal mean is a linear combination L beta of the coefficients with covariance L V L'. Tests and intervals use the standard normal distribution, or a t distribution with the residual degrees of freedom when the model was fitted with test='knha' (the Knapp and Hartung, 2003, https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.1482, adjustment).

docs.title: Reference grid and marginal means
docs.text:
emmprep takes a fitted model (rma_uni, rma_mv, rma_mh, rma_peto, rma_glmm, location-scale and selection models) and builds the reference grid: every combination of factor levels, with the numeric moderators at their mean. emmeans averages the grid over the factors that are not in specs.

from metafopy import contrast, datasets, emmeans, emmprep, escalc, pairs, rma

dat = escalc(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ alloc + ablat', data=dat)
grid = emmprep(res)
print(grid)

     alloc ablat prediction     SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
 alternate 33.46    -0.6195 0.2935 Inf    -1.195  -0.04416
    random 33.46     -0.887 0.1912 Inf    -1.262   -0.5123
systematic 33.46     -0.561 0.2443 Inf     -1.04  -0.08215

Results are given on the log (not the response) scale.
Confidence level used: 0.95

emmprep knows the link from the effect size measure (log for the ratio measures, logit for PLO, and so on), so type='response' back-transforms the estimates and the intervals; the tests stay on the link scale.

means = emmeans(grid, 'alloc')
print(means.summary(type='response'))

     alloc response      SE  df asymp.LCL asymp.UCL
 alternate   0.5382   0.158 Inf    0.3028    0.9568
    random   0.4119 0.07875 Inf    0.2832    0.5991
systematic   0.5706  0.1394 Inf    0.3535    0.9211

Confidence level used: 0.95
Intervals are back-transformed from the log scale

emmeans(res, 'alloc') on a fitted model calls emmprep first; at and cov_reduce set the covariate values, and tran overrides the link. Several variables ('alloc', ['alloc', 'year']) give their cross-classification, and by= gives separate sets of means.

docs.title: Contrasts and multiplicity adjustment
docs.text:
pairs and contrast take the contrast families of emmeans: pairwise, revpairwise, trt_vs_ctrl, trt_vs_ctrlk, eff, del_eff, consec, mean_chg, poly and identity, or a dict of coefficient vectors. Each family has the default adjustment of emmeans (pairwise: Tukey, trt_vs_ctrl: Dunnett, eff: FDR, consec: multivariate t, poly: none), and summary(adjust=...) accepts tukey, dunnettx, sidak, scheffe, mvt and every method of p_adjust. Contrasts of log means show as ratios, contrasts of logit means as odds ratios.

print(pairs(means).summary(type='response'))
print(contrast(means, 'trt_vs_ctrl', ref='alternate').summary(type='response'))

              contrast  ratio     SE  df null z.ratio p.value
    alternate / random  1.307 0.4579 Inf    1  0.7633  0.7255
alternate / systematic 0.9432  0.358 Inf    1  -0.154  0.9870
   random / systematic 0.7218 0.2241 Inf    1   -1.05  0.5452

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates
Tests are performed on the log scale
              contrast  ratio     SE  df null z.ratio p.value
    random / alternate 0.7653 0.2682 Inf    1 -0.7633  0.6577
systematic / alternate   1.06 0.4024 Inf    1   0.154  0.9750

P value adjustment: dunnettx method for 2 tests
Tests are performed on the log scale

The Tukey adjustment is an exact port of R's ptukey/qtukey, and the Dunnett one follows Lund and Lund (1983), https://doi.org/10.2307/2347946. The mvt adjustment integrates the multivariate t distribution with SciPy's quasi-Monte Carlo routine and so agrees with R to about 1e-3 only. See Differences from metafor.

docs.title: Other options
docs.text:
• weights sets how the other factors are averaged: 'equal', 'proportional', 'outer', 'cells', 'flat', a numeric vector with one weight per combination of the averaged factors, or a matrix with one row per row of the result (the rows are recycled and each is scaled to sum to one, as in emmeans).
  • summary(bias_adjust=True, sigma=...) applies the second-order bias adjustment of the back-transformation (emmeans' bias.adjust); sigma defaults to the estimate of tau (0 for rma_mv and location-scale fits).
  • regrid(grid) re-expresses a grid on the response scale with the delta method (bias_adjust=True, sigma=... for the bias adjustment).
  • summary(by=..., cross_adjust=...) adjusts the p-values within each by group and across the groups.

docs.title: One-sided, equivalence and non-inferiority tests
docs.text:
summary, emmeans, contrast and pairs take null, delta and side, as in emmeans. side is '<', '>', '!=', '=' (or -1, 1, 0 and the words 'left', 'right', 'both', 'equivalence', 'noninferiority', 'nonsuperiority', 'inferiority', 'superiority'), and delta is the threshold. A one-sided test has a one-sided interval, with an infinite limit; tukey, scheffe and dunnettx adjustments change to sidak, as emmeans does. With delta > 0 and no side, the test is the equivalence test of Schuirmann (1987, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01068419): the p-value is that of the larger of the two one-sided tests. Values given to emmeans, contrast or pairs are stored in the result and used by its summary unless overridden there.

print(pairs(means).summary(side='>', adjust='none'))
print(pairs(means).summary(delta=0.5, adjust='none'))

docs.title: Nested factors
docs.text:
A factor B is nested in A when each level of B occurs with one level of A only (or when the model has A:B without a main effect of B). emmprep finds such nesting from the data and the model terms (nesting='auto'), hides the combinations that cannot occur, and emmeans averages B within A. contrast and pairs then work within each level of A, and the groups can differ in size, so the multiplicity adjustment is that of the largest family ("(varies)" in the message of R). Give the structure yourself with nesting='B %in% A' (or {'B': 'A'}), or turn the detection off with nesting=None. See the emmeans vignette on nesting and Chambers and Hastie (1992), Statistical Models in S, chapter 2.

# docs: skip
res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ lat + lat:grp', data=dat)  # grp is nested in lat
grid = emmprep(res)  # nesting={'grp': ('lat',)} is detected
print(emmeans(grid, 'grp').summary())
print(pairs(emmeans(grid, 'grp')).summary())  # comparisons within each level of lat

docs.title: Plot gallery
docs.text:
This page reproduces plots of the plot gallery of the metafor project, with the same datasets and the same models. The figures are drawn by metafopy from the code shown with each of them (Viechtbauer, 2010, https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v036.i03). For the figures of metafopy next to those of R metafor 5.2-1, see Plots compared with metafor.

The Python code of each figure is run by the test suite, so it cannot rot. The figures are rendered with python bin/gallery.py and Rscript src/tests/r/gallery.R, see Rendering the figures. 

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use('Agg')

import math
import matplotlib.colors
import matplotlib.patches
import matplotlib.pyplot
import numpy
import pandas
import scipy.special
import scipy.stats

from metafopy import (
    addpoly,
    baujat,
    cumul,
    datasets,
    escalc,
    forest,
    funnel,
    gosh,
    influence,
    labbe,
    llplot,
    permutest,
    plot_cumul,
    plot_gosh,
    plot_infl,
    plot_permutest,
    plot_vif,
    predict,
    qqnorm,
    radial,
    regplot,
    regtest,
    rma,
    rma_mv,
    set_seed,
    trimfill,
    vcalc,
    vif,
)

matplotlib.rcParams['mathtext.default'] = 'regular'
DPI = 100  # the R figures are rendered at the same size and resolution


def pvalue(p: float) -> str:
    """A p-value as metafor's fmtp2 writes it."""
    if p < 0.001:
        return 'p < .001'
    return f'p = {p:.3f}'.replace('0.', '.') if p < 0.1 else f'p = {p:.2f}'.replace('0.', '.')


def fit_stats(text: str, fit) -> str:
    """The label of a model with its Q-test, I^2 and tau^2 (the helper `mlabfun` of the metafor pages)."""
    return f'{text} (Q = {fit.QE:.2f}, df = {fit.k - fit.p}, {pvalue(fit.QEp)}; $I^2$ = {fit.I2:.1f}%, $\\tau^2$ = {fit.tau2:.2f})'

docs.title: Forest plots
docs.text:
All forest plots of this section use the BCG vaccine data.

dat = escalc(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
dat['slab'] = dat['author'] + ', ' + dat['year'].astype(str)
res = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat, slab=dat['slab'])
counts = dat[['tpos', 'tneg', 'cpos', 'cneg']].to_numpy()

docs.title: Forest plot with extra annotations
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot

fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
forest(
    res,
    ax=ax,
    atransf=numpy.exp,
    at=numpy.log([0.05, 0.25, 1, 4]),
    xlim=(-16, 6),
    ilab=counts,
    ilab_lab=['TB+', 'TB-', 'TB+', 'TB-'],
    ilab_xpos=[-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5],
    cex=0.75,
    header='Author(s) and Year',
    mlab='',
    shade=True,
)
ax.text(-8.75, res.k + 2.8, 'Vaccinated', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-5.25, res.k + 2.8, 'Control', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-16, -1, fit_stats('RE Model', res), ha='left', va='center', fontsize=7.5)
fig.savefig('forest.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot with adjusted text position
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_with_textpos

fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
forest(
    res,
    ax=ax,
    atransf=numpy.exp,
    at=numpy.log([0.05, 0.25, 1, 4]),
    xlim=(-20, 2),
    ilab=counts,
    ilab_lab=['TB+', 'TB-', 'TB+', 'TB-'],
    ilab_xpos=[-13.5, -12, -10, -8.5],
    cex=0.75,
    header='Author(s) and Year',
    mlab='',
    textpos=(-20, -3.5),
    shade=True,

ax.text(-12.75, res.k + 2.8, 'Vaccinated', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-9.25, res.k + 2.8, 'Control', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-20, -1, fit_stats('RE Model', res), ha='left', va='center', fontsize=7.5)

docs.title: Forest plot with subgroups
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_with_subgroups

The rows argument places the studies of the three allocation groups, and addpoly adds the summary of each group.

fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(8, 7.5))
forest(
    res,
    ax=ax,
    xlim=(-16, 4.6),
    at=numpy.log([0.05, 0.25, 1, 4]),
    atransf=numpy.exp,
    ilab=counts,
    ilab_lab=['TB+', 'TB-', 'TB+', 'TB-'],
    ilab_xpos=[-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5],
    cex=0.75,
    ylim=(-2, 28),
    top=4,
    order=dat['alloc'],
    rows=numpy.r_[3:5, 9:16, 20:24],
    mlab=fit_stats('RE Model for All Studies', res),
    psize=1,
    header='Author(s) and Year',
)
ax.text(-8.75, 27, 'Vaccinated', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-5.25, 27, 'Control', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
for y, label in ((24, 'Systematic Allocation'), (16, 'Random Allocation'), (5, 'Alternate Allocation')):
    ax.text(-16, y, label, ha='left', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold', fontstyle='italic')
for name, row in (('systematic', 18.5), ('random', 7.5), ('alternate', 1.5)):
    sub = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat, subset=(dat['alloc'] == name).to_numpy(), slab=dat['slab'])
    addpoly(sub, ax=ax, row=row, mlab=fit_stats('RE Model for Subgroup', sub))
mods = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ alloc', data=dat)
ax.text(-16, -1.8, f'Test for Subgroup Differences: $Q_M$ = {mods.QM:.2f}, df = {mods.p - 1}, {pvalue(mods.QMp)}', ha='left', va='center', fontsize=7.5)
fig.savefig('forest_subgroups.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot with multiple CIs
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_with_multiple_cis

The plot shows the 95% CIs of the studies as thin lines and the 80% CIs on top of them as thick lines. forest has no line width argument, so the thick lines are drawn with matplotlib, and the pooled estimate is added with a 99% CI.

fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
forest(dat['yi'], dat['vi'], ax=ax, slab=dat['slab'], xlim=(-8, 6), ylim=(-2, len(dat) + 3), psize=1, efac=0, shade=True)
half = scipy.stats.norm.ppf(0.9) * numpy.sqrt(dat['vi'])
ax.hlines(numpy.arange(len(dat), 0, -1), dat['yi'] - half, dat['yi'] + half, color='black', linewidth=3, zorder=5)
addpoly(res, ax=ax, row=-1, level=99, mlab='RE Model (with 99% CI)', annotate=True)
ax.axhline(0, color='black', linewidth=1)
fig.savefig('forest_multiple_cis.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot with superscripts
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_with_superscripts

The trial numbers are added to the study labels as superscripts, which some journals require. R writes the labels as plotmath expressions; in matplotlib they are strings with a mathtext part, $^{...}$.

slab_ref = [f'{s}$^{{{t}}}$' for s, t in zip(dat['slab'], dat['trial'])]
fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(8, 7))
forest(
    res,
    ax=ax,
    atransf=numpy.exp,
    at=numpy.log([0.05, 0.25, 1, 4]),
    xlim=(-16, 6),
    ilab=counts,
    ilab_lab=['TB+', 'TB-', 'TB+', 'TB-'],
    ilab_xpos=[-9.5, -8, -6, -4.5],
    cex=0.75,
    header='Author(s) and Year',
    mlab='',
    slab=slab_ref,
    shade=True,
)
ax.text(-8.75, res.k + 2.8, 'Vaccinated', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-5.25, res.k + 2.8, 'Control', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=7.5, fontweight='bold')
ax.text(-16, -1, fit_stats('RE Model', res), ha='left', va='center', fontsize=7.5)
fig.savefig('forest_superscripts.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot in RevMan style
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_revman

The plot mimics the forest plots of RevMan, the software of the Cochrane Collaboration: the counts, the weights and the risk of bias ratings of the studies next to the odds ratios. The study with no events in either group has a missing log odds ratio (drop00=True); na_action='pass' in forest keeps it in the plot (R: options(na.action='na.pass')). R's par(mar=...) becomes subplots_adjust, and the text that forest does not draw is added in data coordinates.

FONT = 10  # R's default text size at cex = 1, in points


def put(ax, x, y, s, pos=None, size=1.0, bold=False, offset=0.5, **kw):
    """R's text(): pos 2 puts the text to the left of x and pos 4 to the right, with an offset of half a character."""
    ha = {None: 'center', 2: 'right', 4: 'left'}[pos]
    dx = {None: 0.0, 2: -1.0, 4: 1.0}[pos] * offset * size * FONT * 0.6
    return ax.annotate(
        s,
        (x, y),
        xytext=(dx, 0),
        textcoords='offset points',
        ha=ha,
        va='center_baseline',
        fontsize=size * FONT,
        fontweight='bold' if bold else 'normal',
        annotation_clip=False,
        **kw,
    )


dat_r = pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        'author': ['Amore-Coffea', 'Deliciozza', 'Kahve-Paradiso', 'Mama-Kaffa', 'Morrocona', 'Norscafe', 'Oohlahlazza', 'Piazza-Allerta'],
        'year': [2000, 2004, 2002, 1999, 1998, 1998, 1998, 2003],
        'ai': [2, 10, 0, 12, 3, 19, 4, 8],
        'n1i': [31, 40, 0, 53, 15, 68, 35, 35],
        'ci': [10, 9, 0, 9, 1, 9, 2, 6],
        'n2i': [34, 40, 0, 61, 17, 64, 37, 37],
    }
)
# the risk of bias of items A to F: + is low, - is high and ? is unclear
bias = {'A': '?+--+?+?', 'B': '??--??+?', 'C': '?????++?', 'D': '??+-+?++', 'E': '--+-+-++', 'F': '+++++-++'}
dat_r = escalc(measure='OR', ai='ai', n1i='n1i', ci='ci', n2i='n2i', data=dat_r, drop00=True)
dat_r['slab'] = dat_r['author'] + ' ' + dat_r['year'].astype(str)
res_r = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat_r, method='DL', slab=dat_r['slab'])
pred_r = predict(res_r, transf=numpy.exp)
k = len(dat_r)
weights_r = [''] * k
for i, w in zip(numpy.flatnonzero(res_r.data.keep), res_r.weights_()):
    weights_r[i] = f'{w:.1f}%'

fig = matplotlib.pyplot.figure(figsize=(9.13, 4.71))
ax = fig.add_axes((0, 2.18 / 4.71, 1 - 0.26 / 9.13, 1 - 2.18 / 4.71 - 0.36 / 4.71))
sav = forest(
    res_r,
    ax=ax,
    na_action='pass',
    atransf=numpy.exp,
    at=numpy.log([0.01, 0.10, 1, 10, 100]),
    xlim=(-30, 11),
    xlab='',
    efac=(0, 4),
    textpos=(-30, -4.7),
    lty=('solid', 'solid', 'none'),
    refline=None,
    ilab=numpy.column_stack([dat_r['ai'], dat_r['n1i'], dat_r['ci'], dat_r['n2i'], weights_r]),
    ilab_xpos=[-20.6, -18.6, -16.1, -14.1, -10.8],
    ilab_pos=2,
    cex=0.78,
    header=['Study or Subgroup', 'IV, Random, 95% CI'],
    mlab='',
    colout='#0000cc',
    colci='black',
)
x0, x1 = sav.xlim
ixp = sav.ilab_xpos
cx = sav.cex
ax.plot([x0 + 0.5, x1], [k + 1, k + 1], color='black', linewidth=0.8, clip_on=False)
ax.plot([0, 0], [-2, k + 1], color='black', linewidth=0.8, clip_on=False)

for x, s in zip(ixp, ['Events', 'Total', 'Events', 'Total', 'Weight']):
    put(ax, x, k + 2, s, 2, cx, True)
put(ax, (ixp[0] + ixp[1]) / 2, k + 3, 'Caffeine', 2, cx, True)
put(ax, (ixp[2] + ixp[3]) / 2, k + 3, 'Decaf', 2, cx, True)
put(ax, sav.textpos[1], k + 3, 'Odds ratio', 2, cx, True)
put(ax, 0, k + 3, 'Odds ratio', None, cx, True)
put(ax, x1 - 0.6, k + 3, 'Risk of Bias', 2, cx, True)
put(ax, 0, k + 2, 'IV, Random, 95% CI', None, cx, True)
for x, s, pos in [(x0, 'Total (95% CI)', 4), (ixp[1], str(dat_r['n1i'].sum()), 2), (ixp[3], str(dat_r['n2i'].sum()), 2), (ixp[4], '100.0%', 2)]:
    put(ax, x, -1, s, pos, cx, True)
put(ax, x0, -7, 'Risk of bias legend', 4, cx, True)

# hide the summary estimate of forest and add it back in bold
ax.add_patch(matplotlib.patches.Rectangle((sav.textpos[1], -1.5), ixp[4] - sav.textpos[1], 1, facecolor='white', edgecolor='none', zorder=4))
pe, lo, hi = pred_r.pred[0], pred_r.ci_lb[0], pred_r.ci_ub[0]
put(ax, sav.textpos[1], -1, f'{pe:.2f} [{lo:.2f},  {hi:.2f}]', 2, cx, True, zorder=5)

put(ax, math.log(0.01), -4, 'Favours caffeine', 4, cx, offset=-0.5)
put(ax, math.log(100), -4, 'Favours decaf', 2, cx, offset=-0.5)
put(ax, sav.textpos[1], k + 1 - (numpy.flatnonzero(numpy.isnan(dat_r['yi'])) + 1)[0], 'Not estimable', 2, cx)
put(ax, x0, -2, 'Total events:', 4, cx)
put(ax, ixp[0], -2, str(dat_r['ai'].sum()), 2, cx)
put(ax, ixp[2], -2, str(dat_r['ci'].sum()), 2, cx)
put(
    ax,
    x0,
    -3,
    f'Heterogeneity: Tau$^2$ = {res_r.tau2:.2f}; Chi$^2$ = {res_r.QE:.2f}, df = {res_r.k - res_r.p} (P = {res_r.QEp:.2f}); $I^2$ = {round(res_r.I2)}%',
    4,
    cx,
)
put(ax, x0, -4, f'Test for overall effect: Z = {res_r.zval[0]:.2f} (P = {res_r.pval[0]:.2f})', 4, cx)
put(ax, x0, -5, 'Test for subgroup differences: Not applicable', 4, cx)

colors = {'+': '#00cc00', '-': '#cc0000', '?': '#eeee00'}
for letter, xp in zip('ABCDEF', numpy.linspace(x1 - 5.5, x1 - 0.5, 6)):
    ax.scatter([xp] * k, numpy.arange(k, 0, -1), s=130, color=[colors[c] for c in bias[letter]], clip_on=False, zorder=3)
    for y, c in zip(range(k, 0, -1), bias[letter]):
        put(ax, xp, y, c, None, cx, True, zorder=4)
    put(ax, xp, k + 2, letter, None, cx, True)
for y, s in zip(
    range(-8, -14, -1),
    [
        '(A) Random sequence generation (selection bias)',
        '(B) Allocation concealment (selection bias)',
        '(C) Blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias)',
        '(D) Incomplete outcome data (attrition bias)',
        '(E) Selective reporting (reporting bias)',
        '(F) Other bias',
    ],
):
    put(ax, x0, y, s, 4, cx)
fig.savefig('forest_revman.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot in BMJ style
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_bmj

The plot mimics the forest plots of the BMJ, for the risk differences of the studies of Goldenberg et al. (2021), https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.m4743: the studies are drawn as diamonds sized by their weights, with the CI lines, the vertical reference lines and the summary polygon in the colours of the journal. The CI lines and markers are drawn again on top of those of forest, as in R. (put is the helper of the RevMan plot above.)

dat_b = pandas.DataFrame(
    {
        'author': ['Dyson', 'Jönsson', 'Morris', 'Saslow', 'Saslow', 'Sato', 'Tay', 'Yamada'],
        'year': [2010, 2009, 2019, 2014, 2017, 2017, 2014, 2014],
        'ai': [3, 6, 11, 8, 6, 4, 36, 2],
        'n1i': [6, 6, 21, 9, 11, 22, 46, 12],
        'ci': [1, 3, 0, 5, 0, 0, 30, 2],
        'n2i': [6, 6, 12, 13, 8, 27, 47, 12],
    }
)
dat_b = escalc(measure='RD', ai='ai', n1i='n1i', ci='ci', n2i='n2i', data=dat_b, addyi=False)
dat_b['slab'] = '  ' + dat_b['author'] + ' ' + dat_b['year'].astype(str)
res_b = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat_b, method='DL', slab=dat_b['slab'])
colp, coll = '#5f4c9a', '#a7a9ac'
k = len(dat_b)
wts = res_b.weights_()
psize = 1.2 + (wts - wts.min()) / (wts.max() - wts.min())
rows = numpy.arange(k, 0, -1)
half = scipy.stats.norm.ppf(0.975) * numpy.sqrt(dat_b['vi'])

fig = matplotlib.pyplot.figure(figsize=(10.51, 3.9))
ax = fig.add_axes((3.2 / 10.51 * 0.2, 2.7 / 3.9 * 0.2, 1 - 1.3 / 10.51 * 0.2 - 3.2 / 10.51 * 0.2, 1 - 2.5 / 3.9 * 0.2 - 2.7 / 3.9 * 0.2))
sav = forest(
    dat_b['yi'],
    dat_b['vi'],
    ax=ax,
    xlim=(-3.4, 2.1),
    ylim=(-1, k + 3),
    alim=(-1, 1),
    cex=0.88,
    header=False,
    pch=18,
    psize=psize,
    efac=0,
    refline=None,
    lty=('solid', 'none'),
    xlab='',
    slab=dat_b['slab'],
    ilab=numpy.column_stack(
        [dat_b['ai'].astype(str) + ' / ' + dat_b['n1i'].astype(str), dat_b['ci'].astype(str) + ' / ' + dat_b['n2i'].astype(str), [f'{w:.1f}' for w in wts]]
    ),
    ilab_xpos=[-1.9, -1.3, 1.2],
    annosym=(' (', ' to ', ')'),
    rowadj=-0.07,
)
x0, x1 = sav.xlim
ixp = sav.ilab_xpos
cx = sav.cex
ax.plot([0, 0], [-1, k + 1.6], color=coll, linewidth=1, clip_on=False)
ax.plot([res_b.beta[0]] * 2, [0, k], color=colp, linewidth=0.8, linestyle=(0, (3, 3)))
ax.hlines(rows, dat_b['yi'] - half, dat_b['yi'] + half, color=colp, linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
ax.scatter(dat_b['yi'], rows, marker='D', s=(psize * 1.15 * 6.3) ** 2 / 2, color='white', zorder=4)
ax.scatter(dat_b['yi'], rows, marker='D', s=(psize * 6.3) ** 2 / 2, color=colp, zorder=5)
addpoly(res_b, ax=ax, row=0, mlab='Total (95% CI)', efac=2, col=colp, border=colp)
ax.plot([x0, x1], [k + 1.6] * 2, color=coll, linewidth=1, clip_on=False)
ax.spines['bottom'].set_color(coll)
ax.tick_params(axis='x', color=coll, direction='in', pad=1)

put(ax, x0, k + 2.5, 'Study or\nsubgroup', 4, cx, True, offset=0.5)
put(ax, ixp[0], k + 2.3, 'Experimental', None, cx, True)
put(ax, ixp[1], k + 2.3, 'Control', None, cx, True)
put(ax, (ixp[0] + ixp[1]) / 2, k + 3.4, 'No of events / total', None, cx, True)
put(ax, 0, k + 2.7, 'Risk difference, IV,\nrandom (95% CI)', None, cx, True)
ax.plot([ixp[0] - 0.24, ixp[1] + 0.14], [k + 2.8] * 2, color='black', linewidth=1, clip_on=False)
put(ax, ixp[2], k + 2.7, 'Weight\n(%)', None, cx, True)
put(ax, x1 - 0.37, k + 2.7, 'Risk difference, IV,\nrandom (95% CI)', None, cx, True)
put(ax, -1, -2.5, 'Favors control', 4, cx, True, offset=-0.3)
put(ax, 1, -2.5, 'Favors experimental', 2, cx, True, offset=-0.3)
put(ax, ixp[2], 0, '100.0', None, cx)
put(ax, ixp[0], 0, f'{dat_b["ai"].sum()} / {dat_b["n1i"].sum()}', None, cx)
put(ax, ixp[1], 0, f'{dat_b["ci"].sum()} / {dat_b["n2i"].sum()}', None, cx)
put(
    ax,
    x0,
    -1,
    f'Test for heterogeneity: $\\tau^2$={res_b.tau2:.2f}; $\\chi^2$={res_b.QE:.2f}, df={res_b.k - res_b.p}, P={res_b.QEp:.2f}; $I^2$={round(res_b.I2)}%',
    4,
    cx,
)
put(ax, x0, -2, f'Test for overall effect: Z={res_b.zval[0]:.2f}, P<0.001', 4, cx)
fig.savefig('forest_bmj.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Funnel plot with limit estimate
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:funnel_plot_with_limit_estimate

The regression lines of the regression test for funnel plot asymmetry (regtest, Egger et al., 1997, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.315.7109.629) are added with matplotlib.

res_l = rma('yi', 'vi', data=datasets.load('dat.hackshaw1998'), measure='OR')
fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(7, 7))
funnel(res_l, ax=ax, refline=0)
se = numpy.linspace(0, 0.8, 100)
reg = regtest(res_l, ret_fit=True)
ax.plot(reg.fit.beta[0] + reg.fit.beta[1] * se, se, color='black', linewidth=1, label='Standard Errors as Predictor')
reg = regtest(res_l, predictor='vi', ret_fit=True)
ax.plot(reg.fit.beta[0] + reg.fit.beta[1] * se**2, se, color='black', linewidth=2, linestyle=':', label='Sampling Variances as Predictor')
ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=9, framealpha=1)
fig.savefig('funnel_limit.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Caterpillar plot
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:caterpillar_plot

The data are simulated as on the metafor page, but with the random number generator of NumPy, so the points are not those of the R figure.

rng = numpy.random.default_rng(5132)
k = 250
vi = rng.chisquare(1, k) * 0.03
yi = rng.normal(rng.normal(0.5, 0.4, k), numpy.sqrt(vi))
res_c = rma(yi, vi)
fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(6, 8))
forest(
    yi,
    vi,
    ax=ax,
    header=False,
    xlim=(-2.5, 3.5),
    ylim=(-8, 254),
    order='obs',
    slab=numpy.nan,
    annotate=False,
    efac=(0, 1),
    pch=19,
    colci='gray40',
    psize=2.5,
    cex_lab=1,
    cex_axis=1,
    lty=['solid', 'blank'],
)
addpoly(res_c, ax=ax, mlab='', cex=1)
ax.text(-2, -2, 'RE Model', ha='left', va='center')
fig.savefig('caterpillar.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot with grouped estimates
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_with_grouped_estimates

The effect sizes of a study are drawn on rows close to each other, in a colour per study.

dat_a = datasets.load('dat.assink2016')
V = vcalc(vi=dat_a['vi'], cluster=dat_a['study'], obs=dat_a['esid'], rho=0.6)
res_a = rma_mv(yi='yi', V=V, random='~ 1 | study/esid', data=dat_a)
dat_a = dat_a.sort_values(['study', 'yi'], ascending=False, ignore_index=True)
dat_a['row'] = dat_a['study'].rank(method='dense')
offsets = {1: [0.0], 2: [-0.1, 0.1]}
dat_a['row_seq'] = dat_a['row'] + dat_a.groupby('study')['row'].transform(
    lambda x: pandas.Series(offsets.get(len(x), numpy.linspace(-0.3, 0.3, len(x))), index=x.index)
)
dat_a['slab'] = numpy.where(dat_a['study'].duplicated(), '', 'Study ' + dat_a['study'].astype(str))
palette = matplotlib.colormaps['Dark2'].colors
dat_a['colpt'] = [matplotlib.colors.to_hex(palette[i % len(palette)]) for i in pandas.factorize(dat_a['study'])[0]]
dat_a['colci'] = [matplotlib.colors.to_hex(c, keep_alpha=True)[:7] + '80' for c in dat_a['colpt']]
fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(7, 9))
forest(
    dat_a['yi'],
    dat_a['vi'],
    ax=ax,
    rows=dat_a['row_seq'],
    slab=numpy.nan,
    annotate=False,
    xlim=(-4.4, 4.2),
    ylim=(-2.0, dat_a['row'].max() + 2.5),
    cex=1,
    pch=19,
    psize=0.8,
    efac=0,
    col=list(dat_a['colpt']),
    colci=list(dat_a['colci']),
)
for row, label in zip(dat_a['row'], dat_a['slab'], strict=True):
    ax.text(-4.4, row, label, ha='left', va='center_baseline', fontsize=10)
for h in numpy.arange(0, dat_a['row'].max() + 1) + 0.5:
    ax.axhline(h, color='0.2', linewidth=0.2)
addpoly(res_a, ax=ax, row=-0.25, efac=1, mlab='Pooled Estimate', predstyle='bar')
ax.axhline(0.5, color='black', linewidth=1)
fig.savefig('forest_grouped.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Forest plot in orchard style
docs.text:
Source: https://www.metafor-project.org/doku.php/plots:forest_plot_orchard_style

The correlations of the phylogenetic meta-analysis of Moura et al. (2021) are shown per subphylum, with the points of the studies jittered, and the estimates, CIs and prediction intervals of the model on top.

# docs: skip (the fit takes about a minute and a half; bin/gallery.py runs this block)
dat_m = escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri='ri', ni='ni', data=datasets.load('dat.moura2021'))
levels = sorted(dat_m['subphylum'].unique())
nlvls = len(levels)
res_m = rma_mv('yi', 'vi', mods='~ 0 + subphylum', random=['~ subphylum | study.id', '~ subphylum | effect.size.id'], struct='DIAG', sparse=True, data=dat_m)

# the studies closer to the pooled estimates are jittered more
rng = numpy.random.default_rng(1234)
dat_m['row'] = dat_m['subphylum'].map({name: i + 1 for i, name in enumerate(levels)})
d = numpy.abs(res_m.residuals()) ** (1 / 8)
d = (1 - (d - d.min()) / (d.max() - d.min())) * 0.5
dat_m['row_jitter'] = dat_m['row'] + rng.uniform(-d, d)
palette = matplotlib.colormaps['Dark2'].colors
cols = [matplotlib.colors.to_hex(palette[i % len(palette)]) for i in range(nlvls)]
dat_m['colpt'] = [matplotlib.colors.to_hex(cols[r - 1]) + '99' for r in dat_m['row']]
dat_m['viadj'] = numpy.maximum(dat_m['vi'], dat_m['vi'].quantile(0.05))

fig, ax = matplotlib.pyplot.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
forest(
    dat_m['yi'],
    dat_m['viadj'],
    ax=ax,
    header='Subphylum',
    rows=dat_m['row_jitter'],
    slab=numpy.nan,
    annotate=False,
    xlim=(-1.8, 1.5),
    ylim=(0.5, nlvls + 2.5),
    cex=1,
    pch=19,
    efac=0,
    col=list(dat_m['colpt']),
    colci='none',
    transf=numpy.tanh,
    digits=1,
    xlab='Correlation Coefficient',
)
for i, name in enumerate(levels, start=1):
    ax.text(-1.8, i, name, ha='left', va='center_baseline', fontsize=10)
for h in numpy.arange(0, nlvls + 1) + 0.5:
    ax.axhline(h, color='0.2', linewidth=0.2)

# points, CIs and PIs of the subphylum levels
pred = predict(res_m, newmods=numpy.eye(res_m.p), tau2_levels=list(range(nlvls)), gamma2_levels=list(range(nlvls)), transf=numpy.tanh)
ypos = numpy.arange(1, nlvls + 1)
ax.hlines(ypos, pred.pi_lb, pred.pi_ub, color='black', linewidth=1)
ax.hlines(ypos, pred.ci_lb, pred.ci_ub, color='black', linewidth=3)
ax.scatter(pred.pred, ypos, s=70, facecolor=cols, edgecolor='black', linewidth=1, zorder=5)
ax.text(1.5, nlvls + 1.5, 'k', ha='right', va='center_baseline', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
for i, name in enumerate(levels, start=1):
    ax.text(1.5, i, str((dat_m['subphylum'] == name).sum()), ha='right', va='center_baseline', fontsize=7.5)
fig.savefig('forest_orchard.png', dpi=DPI)

docs.title: Rendering the figures
docs.text:
The image files are committed under docs/images/gallery. To render them again, from the repository root:

source bin/activate.sh
python bin/gallery.py
LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 Rscript src/tests/r/gallery.R

The first command writes docs/images/gallery/py, the second docs/images/gallery/r (it needs R with metafor 5.2-1 and metadat). The R figures are shown on Plots compared with metafor.

docs.title: Fitting models
docs.text:
rma_uni (alias rma) fits equal-effects, fixed-effects, random-effects and mixed-effects (meta-regression) models. It mirrors metafor's rma.uni.

import numpy

from metafopy import datasets, escalc, rma

dat = escalc(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
res = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat)
print(res)

Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.3132 (SE = 0.1664)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5597
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   92.22%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  12.86

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 12) = 152.2330, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se     zval    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub
 -0.7145  0.1798  -3.9744  <.0001  -1.0669  -0.3622  ***

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

docs.title: Ways to give the data
docs.text:
All of these fit the same model:

a = rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat)
b = rma(yi=dat['yi'], vi=dat['vi'])
c = rma(yi=dat['yi'], sei=numpy.sqrt(dat['vi']))
d = rma(measure='RR', ai='tpos', bi='tneg', ci='cpos', di='cneg', data=datasets.load('dat.bcg'))
print(a.beta, b.beta, c.beta, d.beta)

[-0.71453235] [-0.71453235] [-0.71453235] [-0.71453235]

The last form lets rma call escalc for you. It takes the same add, to, drop00 and vtype arguments.

docs.title: The model and the estimator
docs.text:
The model is chosen by method. 'EE' (aliases 'FE' and 'CE') is the equal-effects model. Every other value is a random-effects model with that estimator of the amount of heterogeneity tau^2:

method Estimator 'REML' (default) Restricted maximum likelihood 'ML' Maximum likelihood 'DL', 'DLIT' DerSimonian-Laird, and its iterative version 'HE' Hedges 'HS', 'HSk' Hunter-Schmidt, and its small-sample variant 'SJ', 'SJIT' Sidik-Jonkman, and its iterative version 'EB' Empirical Bayes 'PM' (alias 'MP'), 'PMM' Paule-Mandel, and its median-unbiased version 'GENQ', 'GENQM' Generalized Q-statistic estimators (Jackson, 2013)

Viechtbauer (2005), https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986030003261, and Veroniki et al. (2016), https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1164, compare them. metafopy.models.tau2.ESTIMATORS lists all of them. A list such as method=['REML', 'DL'] tries each in turn until one converges. Optimiser settings go in control=, a Control instance or a dict with metafor's names (tau2_init, tau2_min, tau2_max, threshold, maxiter, stepadj...).

docs.title: Tests and intervals
docs.text:
By default the pooled estimate has a z-test and Wald-type confidence interval. Use test='knha' for the Knapp-Hartung adjustment (a t-test with a rescaled variance; Knapp and Hartung, 2003, https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.1482), which has better coverage with few studies:

print(rma('yi', 'vi', data=dat, test='knha'))

Random-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of total heterogeneity): 0.3132 (SE = 0.1664)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):      0.5597
I^2 (total heterogeneity / total variability):   92.22%
H^2 (total variability / sampling variability):  12.86

Test for Heterogeneity:
Q(df = 12) = 152.2330, p-val < .0001

Model Results:

estimate      se     tval  df    pval    ci.lb    ci.ub
 -0.7145  0.1808  -3.9522  12  0.0019  -1.1084  -0.3206  **

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

level is the confidence level in percent (default 95), and digits controls how much is printed.

docs.title: Meta-regression
docs.text:
Moderators are given as a formula in mods, evaluated on data with formulaic (R-style syntax: '~ ablat + year', '~ C(alloc)', '~ ablat * year'). As in R, factor(), relevel(x, ref) and scale() (which skips missing values) can be used in the formula, as can functions defined in the calling code (they are looked up where rma is called). The same goes for the scale formula of location-scale models.

res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ ablat + year', data=dat)
print(res)

Mixed-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau^2 (estimated amount of residual heterogeneity):     0.1108 (SE = 0.0845)
tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.3328
I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 71.98%
H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   3.57
R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            64.63%

Test for Residual Heterogeneity:
QE(df = 10) = 28.3251, p-val = 0.0016

Test of Moderators (coefficients 2:3):
QM(df = 2) = 12.2043, p-val = 0.0022

Model Results:

         estimate       se     zval    pval     ci.lb    ci.ub
intrcpt   -3.5455  29.0959  -0.1219  0.9030  -60.5724  53.4814
ablat     -0.0280   0.0102  -2.7371  0.0062   -0.0481  -0.0080  **
year       0.0019   0.0147   0.1299  0.8966   -0.0269   0.0307

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Categorical moderators are coded with treatment contrasts, so the intercept is the first level. Use '~ alloc - 1' for one coefficient per level. rma also accepts yi='yi ~ ablat', and a model matrix as mods.

The coefficients are res.beta, in the order of res.coef_names. btt selects the coefficients that the omnibus test tests. It takes 0-based positions (or a regular expression matched against the names):

res = rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ alloc + ablat', data=dat)
print(res.coef_names)
print(rma('yi', 'vi', mods='~ alloc + ablat', data=dat, btt=[1, 2]))

('intrcpt', 'allocrandom', 'allocsystematic', 'ablat')

Mixed-Effects Model (k = 13; tau^2 estimator: REML)

tau (square root of estimated tau^2 value):             0.3803
I^2 (residual heterogeneity / unaccounted variability): 70.11%
H^2 (unaccounted variability / sampling variability):   3.35
R^2 (amount of heterogeneity accounted for):            53.84%

Test for Residual Heterogeneity:
QE(df = 9) = 26.2034, p-val = 0.0019

Test of Moderators (coefficients 2:3):
QM(df = 2) = 1.2850, p-val = 0.5260

allocrandom       -0.2675  0.3504  -0.7633  0.4453  -0.9543   0.4193
